name: LL-37
used_for: LL-37 is the active fragment of the human cathelicidin protein, part of innate immune defense. It has been studied as a topical treatment for chronic leg ulcers (early trials showed mixed results) and in one tiny melanoma injection study. It is promoted online for immunity, infection and healing, including by injection, for which no published human trial was found.

entries.text: Topical LL-37 applied twice weekly for 4 weeks at 0.5, 1.6 or 3.2 mg/mL versus placebo. Healing improved at the 0.5 and 1.6 mg/mL concentrations but not at 3.2 mg/mL (small trial).
entries.population: 34 adults with hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers

entries.text: Topical LL-37 at 0.5 or 1.6 mg/mL with compression therapy versus placebo; no significant overall benefit was found.
entries.population: 148 adults with hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers

entries.text: Registered trial design: LL-37 cream 0.5 mg/mL twice weekly for 4 weeks versus placebo cream; no results are posted.
entries.population: Planned 40 adults with diabetic foot ulcers (Indonesia)

entries.text: Registered trial: LL-37 injected into tumors, starting at 250 micrograms per tumor once weekly for up to 8 weeks, with a second cohort at 500 micrograms per tumor.

internet_entries.text: A dosing-guide site with a supplier shop link says LL-37 is commonly described at 125 mcg daily by subcutaneous injection or 50 to 60 mcg twice daily. It also lists a weight-based figure of 50 mcg per kg per day and topical use at 0.5 and 1.6 mg/mL twice weekly.
internet_entries.population: As described by the source, not a study population

administration_guidance.text: A peptide information site that also sells or links to suppliers says LL-37 degrades in solution, so a mixed vial is kept refrigerated and out of light and used promptly rather than stored for weeks, and that no validated human injection protocol exists.
administration_guidance.label: internet

side_effects.text: In a first-in-human trial of topical LL-37 on venous leg ulcers (34 participants), no local or systemic safety concerns were reported.
side_effects.label: research

side_effects.text: In a small melanoma trial of LL-37 injected into tumors (3 participants), no serious adverse events were listed.
side_effects.label: research

side_effects.text: Laboratory and mouse melanoma experiments found LL-37 increased invasion-linked and blood-vessel-promoting factors, raising a theoretical concern about tumor spread. This is animal and cell data, not observed in people.
side_effects.label: research

side_effects.text: A peptide information site that also sells or links to suppliers says reported LL-37 effects are mostly local, namely injection-site redness, swelling, itching or burning, which it links to histamine release from mast cells, and that persistent or spreading reactions are treated as a reason to stop.
side_effects.label: internet

side_effects.text: A medical spa chain's marketing page says the most common effects are temporary injection-site redness, slight swelling or discomfort that resolves within hours, with some patients reporting temporary fatigue.
side_effects.label: internet

internet_claims.claim: A peptide-guide site (which also sells a paid guide) presents LL-37 as an immune, anti-infective and wound-healing peptide used off-label through compounding pharmacies, while stating that the evidence is mostly preclinical and the best human data is for wounds.

A supplement retailer blog presents LL-37 for beginners as an immune, anti-infective and healing peptide that can be stacked with BPC-157 or TB-500, with dosing tips, and says it is sold for research use and is not FDA-approved. The page is on a store site.

A health-testing company guide says LL-37 is not FDA-approved, is available only through compounding, that the best human data is topical wound trials (a phase IIb study), and that LL-37 can also drive disease in rosacea, autoimmune conditions and some cancers.

research.summary: First-in-human randomized, placebo-controlled trial (Wound Repair Regen) of topical LL-37 (0.5, 1.6 or 3.2 mg/mL, twice weekly for 4 weeks) in 34 people with hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers.
research.finding: Healing rate was higher with 0.5 and 1.6 mg/mL than placebo, with no safety concerns, but the 3.2 mg/mL group did not differ from placebo. The trial was small and company-sponsored.

research.summary: Phase IIb randomized, placebo-controlled trial (Wound Repair Regen) of topical LL-37 (0.5 or 1.6 mg/mL) plus compression in 148 people with hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers.
research.finding: The main analysis found no significant improvement in healing compared with placebo. A post hoc (after the fact) analysis found improvement in some subgroups, which is hypothesis-generating only.

research.summary: Phase 1/2 study at MD Anderson Cancer Center of LL-37 injected into melanoma tumors once weekly for up to 8 weeks, completed 2020; results posted 2021.
research.finding: The record lists only 3 participants started in two dose cohorts (250 and 500 micrograms per tumor), one withdrew for lack of efficacy, and no serious adverse events were listed. It is far too small to show safety or benefit.

research.summary: Registered phase 2 randomized trial (University of Indonesia) of LL-37 cream 0.5 mg/mL versus placebo cream in diabetic foot ulcers, planned for 40 patients.
research.finding: No results are posted and the record status is unknown (not updated), so it shows nothing about effectiveness.

research.summary: Laboratory study (J Invest Dermatol) of human skin wounds and organ-cultured human skin using LL-37 antibodies.
research.finding: Natural LL-37 was high in healing wounds and missing from the edge of chronic ulcers, and blocking it slowed re-epithelialization in skin culture. This suggests a role in healing but is not a treatment test.

research.summary: Study (J Clin Invest) of LL-37 in endothelial cells, a chicken-embryo membrane assay, a rabbit limb-ischemia model and mice lacking the LL-37 counterpart (CRAMP).
research.finding: LL-37 promoted new blood vessel growth in these models, and mice lacking CRAMP had poorer wound vascularization. Animal and cell data only.

research.summary: Study (Cancers) of LL-37 in human melanoma tissue, a mouse melanoma model (using the mouse version, CRAMP) and cultured melanoma cells and macrophages.
research.finding: LL-37 staining increased with melanoma stage, and LL-37 increased invasion-linked and blood-vessel-promoting factors in cells and mouse tumors. This raises a theoretical concern that LL-37 could favor tumor spread, shown only in laboratory models.

research.summary: FDA web page on bulk drug substances for compounding that may present significant safety risks (content current as of 22 April 2026, fetched 2026-09-30).
research.finding: Cathelicidin LL-37 appears in the list of substances nominated but withdrawn (previously category 2). The page says compounded LL-37 may pose immunogenicity risk and peptide impurity concerns, and FDA lacks sufficient safety information. This does not make LL-37 an approved drug.

research.summary: Narrative review (Cell Immunol) by Vandamme and colleagues summarizing what is known about LL-37, the human cathelicidin peptide.
research.finding: Describes LL-37 as an antibacterial, antifungal and antiviral peptide that also attracts and modulates immune cells and can promote wound healing and new blood vessel growth. It notes a possible role in cancer.

dose.summary: Not approved. Human trials used LL-37 applied to the skin (0.5 to 1.6 mg/mL) or injected into melanoma tumors, never injected under the skin for general use. Online sources describe 100 to 200 micrograms (mcg) by injection under the skin, which has not been studied.

mechanism.summary: A natural human immune peptide that damages microbe membranes and also signals to immune cells. How these effects work after a person injects it is not known.

items.text: A review describes LL-37 as an antimicrobial peptide that also attracts and modulates immune cells and promotes wound healing and blood vessel growth.
items.label: research

side_effect_groups.title: In trials
side_effect_groups.summary: No safety concerns were reported in a first small skin trial, and no serious events were listed in a 3-person melanoma trial. Neither is enough to show long-term safety.

items.text: In a first-in-human trial of LL-37 applied to venous leg ulcers (34 participants), no local or systemic safety concerns were reported.
items.label: research

items.text: In a small melanoma trial of LL-37 injected into tumors (3 participants), no serious adverse events were listed.
items.label: research

side_effect_groups.title: Online reports
side_effect_groups.summary: Online sources mostly describe injection-site redness, swelling and itching, sometimes with flu-like symptoms or fatigue. These come from sellers and guide sites, not trials.

items.text: A peptide information site that also sells or links to suppliers says reported LL-37 effects are mostly local, namely injection-site redness, swelling, itching or burning, which it links to histamine release from mast cells, and that persistent or spreading reactions are treated as a reason to stop.
items.label: internet

items.text: A medical spa chain's marketing page says the most common effects are temporary injection-site redness, slight swelling or discomfort that resolves within hours, with some patients reporting temporary fatigue.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peaked Labs says injection-site redness, mild irritation and brief swelling are the most frequent reports, and that some people have mild flu-like symptoms in the first 24 to 48 hours.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer lists injection-site redness, warmth, flushing and soreness as common, and headache and mild fatigue as less common.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Warnings
side_effect_groups.summary: Lab and mouse work suggests LL-37 could favor tumor spread, and it is linked to some inflammatory skin diseases. None of this has been tested in people taking it.

items.text: Laboratory and mouse melanoma experiments found LL-37 increased invasion-linked and blood-vessel-promoting factors, raising a theoretical concern about tumor spread. This is animal and cell data, not observed in people.
items.label: research

items.text: Superpower says LL-37 is a recognized psoriasis autoantigen, contributes to inflammation in rosacea, and has been linked to tumor growth in breast, ovarian and lung cancers. It frames these as theoretical concerns.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer lists autoimmune flare risk, neutrophil trap release (NETosis) at high doses, and Herxheimer-like reactions from biofilm breakdown among serious concerns.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Regulator warning
side_effect_groups.summary: The FDA lists LL-37 among compounding substances that may pose significant safety risks. It is not an approved drug.

items.text: The FDA says compounded LL-37 may pose immunogenicity risk and peptide impurity concerns, and that it lacks sufficient safety information.
items.label: research
